## Today's Agenda

- Why only 36 percent of studies could be redone
- Why clicking through menus loses the record, and why code keeps it
- The four tools, and the order to install them
- The setup check
- Your first look at the example data

## Only 36 Percent of Studies Replicated

[Open Science Collaboration, 2015]{.eyebrow}

- 270 researchers set out to redo **100 published psychology studies**
- They used the same methods, similar participants, and the same analyses
- Only **36 percent** replicated at conventional thresholds
- Among those that did, effect sizes were on average **half** the original size
- The result was published in *Science* and is one of the decade's most cited findings

## Two Words From That Study

::: {.define}
**Replication:** running a study again with new data to see whether it reaches the same answer. Example: the 270 researchers redid each study with new participants.
:::

::: {.define}
**Effect size:** how big a difference is, on a scale that does not grow with the sample. Example: the replications found effects about half the size the originals reported.
:::

## The Cause Was Friction, Not Fraud

- Methods sections did not contain enough detail to re-run the analysis
- Researchers had to email the original authors for clarification
- Some authors had moved, and some had lost the data
- Some had used software whose menus had since changed
- The work was never **built to be retraceable** in the first place

## Menus Leave No Record

- SPSS, Excel, and JMP work through menus and dialog boxes
- You click Analyze, then Compare Means, then One-Way ANOVA
- The result appears, and **the click history vanishes**
- To verify your work, a collaborator needs a prose description of every click
- Almost no one writes that description well, and almost no one wants to

The course's VS Code menus are different: each one writes its R code into your script, so the record stays.

## Code Is the Methods Section

- A script is a description of every step, in a language a computer can re-run
- **When you write your analysis as code, the code is the methods section**
- Reinhart and Rogoff was caught because the spreadsheet was eventually shared
- It would have been caught faster if the analysis had been code from the start

::: {.define}
**Reproducibility:** getting the same results again from the same data, the same code, and the same steps. Example: anyone who renders your file on the example data gets your exact message counts.
:::

## Exercise: Could You Rebuild Your Number? {.discuss}

Answer each in writing:

- Think of a number you produced for a class: an average, a count, or a percentage
- State whether you could reconstruct exactly how you got it six months from now
- List what you would have needed to write down at the time

## Four Tools, One Ecology

- **VS Code** is the editor, where prose, code, and notes all live in tabs
- **R** is the language that does the counting and the statistics
- **Quarto** is the publishing system that turns source into finished output
- **Git and GitHub** are version control and a home for the history

All four are free, open, and cross-platform, and each produces a plain-text record of what
you did.

## Why R and Why Quarto

- R dominates social science: communication, sociology, and political science
- Its packages for content analysis, reliability, and regression are the deepest available
- Python is also excellent, and the skills transfer both ways
- Quarto takes one `.qmd` source and produces HTML, PDF, Word, or slides
- The source mixes prose with code, and **the code runs when you render**

## Why Git and GitHub

- Git tracks every change to every file in a project
- GitHub hosts that history on the web, publicly by default
- You get a permanent audit trail and the ability to roll back to any state
- Students get the **GitHub Student Developer Pack** at no cost
- The pack includes **GitHub Copilot**. The course workspace tells Copilot Chat to write tidyverse code with `%>%` and to remind you to log each exchange in your AI-use log
- This is the standard workflow in research labs and industry data teams

## Two Git Words

::: {.define}
**Repository (repo):** a project folder that Git tracks, holding your files and the full history of every change to them. Example: the `mc451-workspace` folder you build on Thursday.
:::

::: {.define}
**Commit:** a saved change to your files in Git, recorded with who made it, when, and a short message saying what changed. Example: "Add my research question to the prospectus."
:::

## Packages and the Tidyverse

::: {.define}
**Package:** a bundle of functions, data, and help pages that adds to what R can do on its own. Example: the course's v2v package adds the example Twitch data and `clean_dates()`.
:::

::: {.define}
**Tidyverse:** a collection of R packages for data science that share one design and are built to work together. Example: `library(tidyverse)` loads its core packages at once, including dplyr for tables and ggplot2 for charts.
:::

## Install Order, Part One

Order matters. Install these first:

1. **R**, from cran.r-project.org, with installer defaults
2. **VS Code**, from code.visualstudio.com
3. **The R extension** for VS Code, by REditorSupport
4. **Quarto**, from quarto.org, installed with defaults

R has no interface of its own. It is a backend that other tools call.

## Install Order, Part Two

5. **The Quarto extension** for VS Code, for live preview of `.qmd` files
6. **Git**, from git-scm.com, with default options
7. **A GitHub account**, with a professional username you will link work to
8. **The `v2v` package**, with the install command on the V2V Hub
9. **The AURA Lab R Companion**, inside VS Code: Extensions view > search AURA Lab R Companion > Install

Click-by-click walkthroughs with screenshots live on the Hub.

## The Setup Check

The starter file `00-check-your-setup.qmd` on the Hub ends by running one chunk:

```r
library(v2v)
v2v::setup()
```

- The validator confirms that R, Quarto, Git, and the packages the course needs are present
- Success prints **Everything the course needs is installed.**
- Then open the Command Palette and run **Check my setup**. It runs the same checklist, and its **Install what is missing** action installs any package it flags
- Anything else means the Hub's troubleshooting page is your next stop

| xqcow | Just Chatting | 19,381 | 1542578200240 |

| sodapoppin | Marble It Up! | 28,076 | 1542578261145 |

## The Data Moves

::: {.define}
**Time series:** a set of measurements of the same thing taken one after another over time. Example: four channels repeat across these ten rows, so each one's viewer count can be followed minute by minute.
:::

- Sodapoppin climbs from 27,934 to 28,076 to 28,203
- That is **269 viewers gained in 122 seconds**

## What Moves the Numbers

- xQc lost 150 viewers and then held steady, Forsen lost 120, and Giantwaffle gained 3
- Each number is a real moment: a clip going viral, or a raid arriving

::: {.define}
**Raid:** on Twitch, a streamer ending a stream by sending their viewers to another live channel. Example: a viewer count that jumps by hundreds in one minute.
:::

## Three More Things to Notice

- **The timestamps look like nonsense:** Chapter 11 shows how to convert them

::: {.define}
**Unix epoch time:** time counted from midnight UTC on January 1, 1970; this data counts it in milliseconds. Example: 1542578200214 is a moment on November 18, 2018.
:::

- **There is a hidden newline** inside sodapoppin's title
    - Real data is messy in exactly this way
- **Titles are themselves data**
    - "No Smoking in Chat" performs etiquette, and Chapter 12 returns to title content

## The v2v Package

The course companion package ships three things:

- **Two fixtures:** `twitch_chat_sample`, roughly 35,000 messages, and `twitch_streams_sample`, roughly 32,000 rows across 50 channels
- **Helper functions** for loading data, codebook skeletons, reliability, and plots
- **The setup validator**, `v2v::setup()`, which you can rerun any time

Load a fixture with `data(twitch_chat_sample, package = "v2v")`.
